messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  (none)

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Miguel

Miguel Santoro was fifty-eight when the warehouse collapsed. He had spent thirty-two years in forensic analysis—meticulous work, methodical, the kind that required him to walk into scenes of chaos and extract order from them. He prided himself on this. His colleagues called him steady. His wife, Rosa, said he was the calmest person she knew. On the morning of March 14th, Miguel was at the Riverside Industrial Complex conducting a post-fire investigation. The building had burned three days earlier; his job was to map the structural damage, photograph the debris field, establish the sequence of collapse. He was on the second floor, taking measurements near what had been the loading dock, when the remaining eastern wall gave way. The sound came first—a deep, tearing crack that seemed to open the air itself. Then the floor beneath him tilted. He had perhaps two seconds to understand what was happening before the concrete and steel came down. He fell through the opening, landing hard on a pile of rubble one story below, his left leg pinned under a metal beam, his right shoulder dislocated. He lay there for forty minutes before the rescue team reached him. The weight of the debris, the dust that made every breath feel like swallowing ash, the knowledge that more of the structure could fail at any moment—these details had fused into something permanent in his nervous system.

Three months later, Miguel still felt the vibration. Not metaphorically. His body remained in a state of constant vigilance, muscles tight across his shoulders and jaw, his startle response so acute that Rosa had learned not to come up behind him unexpectedly. A car door slamming outside the house would send him rigid. The beep of the microwave made him flinch. He had returned to work at the end of May, against Rosa's wishes, because he believed that staying home would mean surrendering to fear, would mean admitting that the collapse had broken something fundamental in him. But within two weeks, he realized that his hands trembled when he held a camera. More troubling was what had begun to happen in his mind. He found himself catastrophizing in ways that felt alien to him—walking into a restaurant and immediately calculating exit routes, noting which structural elements looked compromised, wondering if the ceiling could hold. When his supervisor asked him to investigate a structural fire at a shopping mall, Miguel declined. Then declined again. He told himself it was reasonable caution, but beneath that reasoning was something darker: the conviction that he could no longer trust his own judgment, that whatever instinct had kept him safe for three decades had failed him utterly. If he had missed the signs of imminent collapse at Riverside, how could he possibly assess danger anywhere else?

The avoidance had grown quietly at first. He stopped taking assignments that required him to enter unfamiliar buildings. He began driving familiar routes only, avoiding the highway that passed near construction sites. When Rosa suggested they visit their son in Sacramento—a three-hour drive through terrain Miguel didn't know well—he invented reasons they couldn't go. He couldn't explain to her that the thought of being in a car on an unfamiliar road, unable to assess potential hazards, unable to control the environment, filled him with a dread that felt like drowning. What frightened him most was not the prospect of another disaster, but rather his own incompetence in the face of it. He had come to believe that his reactions since the collapse—the hypervigilance, the avoidance, the constant mental scanning for threats—proved that he was a lousy coper, that a genuinely capable man would have moved past this by now. The man he had been before March 14th would have. That man had been someone Rosa could rely on, someone his colleagues respected, someone whose steadiness was almost legendary. Now, when he looked at his own behavior—the way he'd stopped attending his Thursday night poker game because the bar was in an unfamiliar neighborhood, the way he'd asked to be reassigned to office-based analysis only, the way he'd become someone who couldn't even drive to the grocery store without first mapping the route and checking for construction—he saw only a shell of that person. The world had revealed itself to be far more dangerous than he'd ever allowed himself to believe, and he was no longer the kind of man equipped to navigate it. Rosa had stopped mentioning the trip to Sacramento. She had stopped asking him to go anywhere at all. It was this—the quiet acceptance of his diminishment in her eyes—that finally brought Miguel to his first therapy appointment. He sat in the waiting room, his leg bouncing rhythmically, and wondered if even talking about what happened would prove that he was beyond repair.
